unit.title: Reading a chart
unit.description: Axes, chart types, timeframes, scales, trend and volume

texts: Just a line
Hugo
My investing app only shows me a line. Am I missing something?
What do you tell him?
For looking at years, the line is enough; candles show every session
That's it. The line joins up the closes; candles record all four prices.
Nothing: the line tells you everything
Without candles you can't see highs, lows or what happened during the day.
You can't invest without candles
You can invest well while hardly looking at charts. Candles are useful, not compulsory.
**Bars** go from the low to the high, with two little ticks.
The one on the left is the open; the one on the right, the close.
**Candlesticks** say the same thing with a coloured body. They're the standard.
OK, show me one!

steps.prompt: With candlesticks you can see each day's battle. Tap the longest green candle
steps.ok: It opened near the low and closed near the high: buyers were in charge the whole session. On a line chart you'd just see a higher point.
steps.ko: Look for the tallest green body, with hardly any thin lines above or below.

texts: Line or candles?
Each chart answers a question. Which would you use for each thing?
Line or area
Candles or bars
Seeing how an index fund has done over 10 years
For the long-term trend, the line is enough and easier to read.
Seeing whether the price rose today and then came back down
Only candles and bars record the day's high.
Knowing yesterday's low to set a stop
The line only has closes: you can't see the low.
Comparing two indices over decades
The line shows the direction without the noise.
Reading each day's open and close
They're two of each candle's four prices.
Showing how much your portfolio has grown in 5 years
For a long-term picture, the line or the area chart.
Sort the six uses.
The **line** sums up where it's heading; **candles** tell you who won each period. To trade, you need all four prices.
Is the close enough, or do you need what happened during the day?
Choose the chart for each thing

steps.title: Be careful with Heikin Ashi
steps.body:
There are other kinds too: the **area** chart (the line with the space below filled in, as in lots of apps) and **Heikin Ashi**, averaged candles that smooth out the noise.

Its opens and closes are calculated from averages: **they're not real prices**. It's useful for seeing the trend, never for deciding what price to enter at or where to put a stop.
steps.key: The line sums up; candlesticks tell the story of each period's battle.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Apple and switch from Line to Candles.

texts: The 5-minute chart
Irene
I'm investing in a share for 10 years. On the weekly chart it's been rising for a year.
But today, on the 5-minute chart, it's been falling all morning! Should I sell?
What do you tell her?
Look at the timeframe that matches your horizon
That's it. Over 10 years, the weekly chart is what counts; the morning is noise.
Sell now: the trend has changed
One morning on a 5-minute chart doesn't break a year-long trend.
Buy more to take advantage of the dip
Don't sell or buy because of one morning: it's the wrong tool.
Each candle can be a minute, an hour, a day, a week or a month.
The daily chart can show a rise and the 5-minute chart a fall. Both are true.
Trading every few minutes
On minute charts, **noise** rules: signals are as hit-and-miss as a coin toss. And every trade pays a commission and the *spread*.
A thousand people trade on heads or tails, paying €5 each time. After 300 trades, how many are losing?
Half: it's a coin toss
The vast majority
Almost nobody
**80 %** are losing: the commission tilts the coin against them on every trade.
Get to 300 trades per person and see how many are losing.
The shorter the timeframe, the more trades and the more **costs**. In a study of *day trading* in Brazil (2013-2015), **97 %** of those who kept at it for more than 300 days lost money.
Eight out of ten are losing, and nobody did anything odd.
With one trade, it's fifty-fifty: a coin toss.
Add more trades and watch the losers
Each horizon, its chart
You choose the timeframe according to how long you hold your investments. Which chart suits each person?
Minutes or hours
Daily
Weekly or monthly
Sara opens and closes her trades on the same day
For the same day, minute or hourly candles.
Leo holds his trades for a few weeks
Weeks to months: the daily chart.
Nora checks her pension plan once a year
Over many years: weekly or monthly.
Iván scalps crypto
Trades lasting seconds or minutes.
Eva looks for trades lasting one to three months
Months: the daily chart is hers.
Hugo is investing in an index fund for 20 years
Minute candles would only give him frights.
Place all six people.

Choose the timeframe to suit your **horizon** and always look at **the longer one before the shorter one**. Elder's method: weekly for direction, daily for timing and hourly to fine-tune the entry and the stop. Try it: in Market, open an asset and switch from 1D to 1W to see the big trend.
How long does each person hold their investment?
Place each person
Bitcoin, a flat line
Dani
I've seen a bitcoin chart from 2013. Until 2017 it's a flat line.
Didn't it move before that?
What do you tell him?
It's the linear scale: at low prices, huge percentages take up hardly any space
That's it. On a log scale, +100 % takes up the same space in 2014 as in 2024.
No, nothing happened before then
Loads happened, with falls of more than 80 %. On a linear scale you can't see it.
The chart must be wrong
The chart's fine. What's misleading is a linear scale over so many years.
**Linear:** each centimetre is worth the same number of euros.
**Logarithmic:** each centimetre is worth the same percentage.
On a log scale, €10 to €20 takes up the same space as €100 to €200.
Bitcoin, up and down
Late 2020. You invest **€10,000** in bitcoin. Real data, week by week. Keep an eye on the percentages.
If something falls 75 %, how much does it then need to rise to get back to where it was?
From 100 to 25 is −75 %; to get from 25 back to 100 you have to multiply by 4: **+300 %**.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
Bitcoin fell **75 %** from its 2021 peak and needed to rise **302 %** to get back. Percentages **aren't symmetrical**, and the logarithmic scale respects those proportions; the linear one doesn't.
You've sold. Watch what happens next…
Almost half of what you put in. How much would it take to get it back?
Almost double! Bitcoin moves a lot in both directions.
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
Which scale would you choose?
On long charts, the scale changes what you see. **Logarithmic**, or does it **make little difference**?
Logarithmic
Makes little difference
The Nasdaq 100 since 1985
Four decades and very different prices: logarithmic.
A share this week
Over short stretches, euros and percentages move almost in step.
A crypto that has multiplied by 100
On a linear scale, its early years would look like a flat line.
The euro against the dollar today
A single day: the scale changes almost nothing.
A fund over 40 years
To compare eras, look at percentages.
A share over the last month
Small moves: there's hardly any difference.
Sort the six charts.

For long periods or assets that have multiplied many times over, **logarithmic**. Over short stretches, euros and percentages move almost in step. Try it: in Market, open Bitcoin on 1M and use «Measure» on an old rise and a recent one.
Is it years and very different prices, or just a few days?
Logarithmic or no difference?
Still rising?
Leo
My share was rising: a high of €40, down to €36 and a bounce to €39.
Now it's dropped to €35. Is the uptrend still on?
What do you tell him?
It's in doubt: a lower high and a lower low
Exactly. It didn't beat €40 and it broke below €36.
Yes, it's just a normal pullback
A 5-10 % pullback is normal. But here the structure has broken.
It's definitely going to fall 50 %
Breaking the structure doesn't tell you how far it'll fall. It may go sideways.
**Uptrend:** higher highs and higher lows. **Downtrend:** lower and lower.
Charles Dow put it into words in the late nineteenth century.
Highs and lows
Here are the last three highs and lows on each chart. What's the trend?
Uptrend
Downtrend
Sideways
Highs and lows are both rising.
Both are falling.
They repeat: a ceiling and a floor with no direction.
Each dip stops higher than the last.
The bounces don't reach the previous high.
It bounces between a ceiling and a floor.
Sort the six sequences.
If highs and lows rise, it's an **uptrend**; if both fall, a **downtrend**; if they repeat, **sideways**. A 5-10 % pullback is normal within a healthy rise.
Look at the lows first: are they rising, falling or repeating?
Sort each sequence
Does the trend continue?
Four real charts with a clear direction. Up or down over the next 10 sessions? Does the trend **continue** or **reverse**?
Play all four rounds.
In these four rounds, the trend continued in three and reversed in one. **Momentum** shows up in the data, but it's a probability, not a promise.
Following the trend worked here. It doesn't always.
A trend can reverse without warning.
See where the candles are heading and decide

steps.title: Momentum is real
steps.body: Trends lasting 3–12 months have tended to persist in shares, bonds, currencies and commodities (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993; Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, 2012). Profiting from it after costs and sharp reversals is another story.
steps.key: Uptrend = higher highs and lows; downtrend = lower ones.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Apple on 1W and check whether its lows are rising.

texts: A breakout with few people
Sara
My share has just broken above its high for the year! I'm buying now.
And today's volume?
Half the usual. Does it matter?
What do you tell her?
Yes: wait and see if it closes above it with volume
Good. With high volume, the breakout is far more believable.
No: a breakout is a breakout
Without volume, few people are backing it. It's the classic **false breakout**.
Sell: low volume guarantees a fall
It casts doubt on the breakout, but it guarantees nothing.
**Volume** is what changes hands in each period: the bars at the bottom.
The price tells you what's happening. Volume tells you how many people believe it.
Confirms or casts doubt?
The same price move, with different volume. Does the volume **confirm** it or **cast doubt** on it?
Confirms it
Casts doubt on it
Rises on triple the average volume
Lots of people behind the rise: conviction.
Breaks through resistance on very low volume
Few people behind it: risk of a false breakout.
Rises every day, but on less volume
Possible exhaustion: fewer and fewer people are joining in.
Breaks below support on huge volume
The break has lots of people behind it: more reliable.
Hits a new high on volume well above average
High volume on the breakout: more believable.
Sort the five moves.
A move with lots of volume has **lots of people behind it**. Without volume it can be an illusion, like a **false breakout**.
Are there lots of people behind the move, or just a few?
Confirms or casts doubt?

steps.title: Spikes and limits
steps.body:
• Rises on high volume: conviction. Falls on low volume: a calm pullback.
• Volume spikes come with news, expiries, panic or euphoria; after a sharp fall, they sometimes mark **capitulation**.
• In forex there's no centralised volume, and in crypto it's spread across lots of platforms.
steps.key: A move with lots of volume has lots of people behind it; without volume it may be an illusion.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, find the day with the most volume in the last month.

u19l2-1.prompt: Match each chart type with what it shows.
u19l2-1.explanation: Line and area charts summarise; bars and candlesticks have all four prices; Heikin Ashi smooths things out at the cost of not showing real prices.
right: From low to high, with little ticks for the open and close
A coloured body between the open and the close

u19l2-2.prompt: Which chart doesn't show the real opening and closing prices?
u19l2-2.explanation: Heikin Ashi calculates each candle from averages to smooth out the noise: its opens and closes aren't traded prices.

u19l2-3.prompt: Tap the candle with the biggest green body.
u19l2-3.explanation: That huge body tells you buyers dominated the session from start to finish. A line chart would only show you a higher close. (Apple · daily candles · April 2025)

u19l2-6.prompt: On a line chart, you can see the direction at a glance. What's the trend? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u19l2-6.explanation: Each bounce stops below the previous one and the closes keep getting lower.

u19l2-7.prompt: The chart that smooths out noise using averages is called ____.
u19l2-7.explanation: Heikin Ashi is for seeing the trend; marubozu and doji are types of candle, and Fibonacci is a retracement tool.

u19l2-8.prompt: Pablo is looking at a Heikin Ashi chart, sees that the last candle closed at €102 and places a sell order at exactly that price. What do you tell him?
options: Well done: that's the candle's close
To wait for the Heikin Ashi to turn green
To check the real prices on candlesticks or bars before setting the order
u19l2-8.explanation: Each chart type has its use: Heikin Ashi for the trend, candlesticks or bars for real prices.
feedback: That €102 is a calculated average, not a traded price: his order may not be filled where he thinks.
The colour helps you see the trend, but its prices still aren't real.
That's it: Heikin Ashi is for the trend; for trading prices, look at candlesticks, bars or a line.

u19l3-1.prompt: Rank from most noise to least noise.
u19l3-1.explanation: The shorter the timeframe, the more random, meaningless moves.

u19l3-3.prompt: These closes cover about eight weeks. What trend do you see? (LVMH · closes every 3 sessions · October–November 2025)
u19l3-3.explanation: On this scale, highs and lows are rising. Within those weeks there were down days that would look dramatic on a 5-minute chart.

u19l3-4.prompt: Daily chart of 30 sessions, with no name or date. Up or down over the next 10?
u19l3-4.explanation: Ten sessions is a short horizon, and noise weighs heavily on it. Notice how much it moved and ask yourself whether you'd have held on.

u19l3-5.prompt: Different asset, same challenge. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u19l3-5.explanation: The asset changes, the idea doesn't: in the short term, nobody gets it right reliably just by looking at candles.

u19l3-6.prompt: In the triple screen method, what is the longest timeframe for?
u19l3-6.explanation: The longest one sets the direction: if the weekly is in an uptrend, you only look for buys. The shortest fine-tunes the entry and the stop.

u19l3-11.prompt: Leo holds his trades for a few weeks. On the weekly chart, the stock is making lower highs and lower lows. On the daily, it's rising strongly today. What does he do?
options: Looks at the 1-minute chart to decide
Doesn't look for buys while the weekly is still bearish
Buys now: the daily rules because it's more recent
u19l3-11.explanation: Elder's method: the longer timeframe decides the direction and the shorter one only fine-tunes the entry. Buying against the weekly is swimming against the current.
feedback: Dropping to minutes adds noise, not information: the problem is that it goes against the weekly.
That's it: the longer timeframe first. A strong day inside a weekly decline usually ends up as just a bounce.
The daily fine-tunes the timing, but the weekly sets the direction, and there it's bearish.

u19l4-1.prompt: A share has gone from €1 to €300 in 15 years. Which scale do you use to study its history?
u19l4-1.explanation: On a linear scale, the early years would look like a flat line even if there were 100 % rises. The logarithmic scale shows percentages properly.

u19l4-2.prompt: On a linear scale, rising from 10 to €20 takes up the same space as rising from 100 to €200.
u19l4-2.explanation: That's what happens on a logarithmic scale. On a linear one, 100 to €200 takes up ten times more space than 10 to €20.

u19l4-7.prompt: S&P 500, late September 1929: weekly closes have been rising for almost two years. What do you think happened next?
u19l4-7.explanation: With moves this big, the scale decides what you see: on a hundred-year linear chart, any early stretch looks like a flat line. To compare eras, look at percentages.

u19l4-8.prompt: On a logarithmic scale, the same vertical distance represents the same ____.
u19l4-8.explanation: That's why it's good for comparing eras with very different prices.

u19l4-11.prompt: On a 10-year linear chart, a stock rises from €10 to €20 at the start and from €100 to €200 at the end. Dani says the second rise was much better because it looks ten times bigger. What do you tell him?
options: That the first was better because the stock was cheaper
That he's right: it looks bigger, so it was better
That both were +100 %: on a logarithmic scale they'd take up the same space
u19l4-11.explanation: What matters to your money is the percentage. The linear scale enlarges the stretches with high prices; the logarithmic one compares them properly.
feedback: Being cheaper doesn't make it better: in both stretches the money doubled.
On a linear scale it looks bigger because it's more euros, but in percentage terms both are the same.
That's it: whoever bought at the start also doubled their money. The logarithmic scale shows it as it is.

u19l5-1.prompt: What's the trend on this chart? (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u19l5-1.explanation: Each dip stays above the previous one and each rise beats the previous high.

u19l5-2.prompt: And this one? (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u19l5-2.explanation: The bounces don't reach the previous highs and the lows keep getting lower.

u19l5-3.prompt: And this one? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u19l5-3.explanation: The price goes up and down between a ceiling and a floor; at the end it's almost where it started.

u19l5-4.prompt: In this sideways trend, tap the floor of the range: the lowest close (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u19l5-4.explanation: That's where buyers showed up. If the price comes back to that area, lots of people will be watching it.

u19l5-5.prompt: Highs at 50, 54 and €58; lows at 45, 48 and €52. What trend is it?
u19l5-5.explanation: Rising highs and lows: that's the definition of an uptrend.

u19l5-7.prompt: A share rises for months. It makes a high at €60, falls to €54, bounces only as far as €58 and then falls to €52. What has happened?
options: The uptrend has been called into question
u19l5-7.explanation: According to Dow theory, an uptrend is called into question when it fails to beat the last high and breaks below the last low.
feedback: Exactly: a lower high and a lower low. It doesn't tell you how far it will fall, but it's no longer a clean rise.
A broken structure doesn't tell you how far it will fall: it could turn sideways.
It fails to beat the high (58 < 60) and breaks the low (52 < 54): the uptrend structure is broken.

u19l5-8.prompt: Look at the structure of these 30 daily candles. Up or down over the next 10?
u19l5-8.explanation: Momentum is a statistical tendency over months, not a promise for next week. The structure helps you know where you'd be proved wrong.

u19l6-2.prompt: The price breaks through a resistance level on volume well below average. What's the risk?
u19l6-2.explanation: Without volume, the breakout has few people behind it and it's easier for the price to fall back inside.

u19l6-3.prompt: Match each situation with how it's usually read.
options: Huge spike after a sharp fall
u19l6-3.explanation: These are common readings, not exact rules: volume gives context, not certainties.

u19l6-4.prompt: Tap the candle with the most conviction: a big body and hardly any wicks.
u19l6-4.explanation: It opened almost at the low and closed almost at the high. If it also came on high volume, the sign of strength would be more convincing. (NVIDIA · daily candles · March–April 2026)

u19l6-6.prompt: Without seeing the volume you only have half the story. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u19l6-6.explanation: Even if you could see the volume, a single clue isn't enough to guess the short term. Volume helps you judge whether a move has people behind it.

u19l6-9.prompt: A move with lots of volume has lots of people behind it; one without volume may be ____.
u19l6-9.explanation: Volume measures how many people are backing a move.

u19l6-10.prompt: In which cases is volume data less reliable? Tick all that apply.
options: Indices, depending on how each provider calculates it
Cryptocurrencies, spread across lots of platforms
u19l6-10.explanation: In forex there's no centralised volume, in crypto it's spread out and some of it may be artificial, and for indices it depends on the provider.
